common_name: Betty Woods Daylily (Ruffled Double Gold Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Betty Woods holds its double form and gold color well in Gulf South heat and reliably rebounds after summer flushes of bloom.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; Betty Woods is a long-popular double daylily, producing consistently full, ruffled, cream-to-gold blooms with a green throat that hold their double form far more reliably in heat and humidity than many other double cultivars, which is why it remains a garden and hybridizing standard decades after its introduction. It is a strong, vigorous rebloomer over a long summer season and increases quickly into full, floriferous clumps. Deadhead spent scapes to tidy the planting and encourage continued flowering, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring. Its dependable doubling and heat tolerance make it one of the better double daylilies for Gulf Coast gardens, where many double-flowered cultivars revert to single form under stress.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; this tetraploid cultivar produces heavily ruffled, substantial blooms that benefit from full sun to develop their best color and form.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Something Wonderful is a tetraploid daylily prized for large, heavily ruffled lavender-pink flowers with a contrasting green throat, the ruffled edge giving the bloom exceptional substance and a lightly gold-dusted sheen in bright light. It is a vigorous, floriferous grower that produces well-branched scapes carrying many buds per stem, extending the effective bloom season well beyond a single flush. Remove spent scapes after flowering finishes to keep the clump tidy and redirect energy into the crown for the following year. Divide every three to four years in spring as clumps become congested, replanting divisions promptly to minimize root stress.

common_name: Prairie Blue Eyes Daylily (Lavender-Blue Eyed Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Prairie Blue Eyes is one of the more reliably blue-toned daylilies and keeps its eyezone contrast best with a full day of sun.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Prairie Blue Eyes bears near-white to pale lavender petals overlaid with a distinct lavender-blue eyezone above the green throat, one of the coolest, most blue-leaning color combinations available in daylilies, which otherwise run overwhelmingly toward warm yellows, oranges, and reds. Flowers are held on well-branched scapes above a vigorous, disease-resistant clump that increases readily. It pairs especially well with true-blue or white companion perennials, where its cool eyezone reads as a genuine blue accent in the border. Divide every three to four years in early spring as the clump becomes crowded, and keep plantings consistently watered through summer bloom for the best flower size and color saturation.

common_name: Garden Treasure Itoh Peony (Large Yellow Intersectional Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4–6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates; Itoh peonies tolerate the marginal chill of zone 8b–9 better than straight herbaceous cultivars.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving afternoon shade where summers are hottest. Garden Treasure is one of the most widely grown Itoh (intersectional) peonies, producing an abundance of huge, semi-double golden-yellow blooms with a faint rose flare at the petal base over a long bloom period, since the woody-based, bushy plant carries many buds per stem that open in succession rather than all at once. Like other Itoh hybrids its sturdy stems support the heavy flowers without staking and the attractive, deeply cut foliage remains clean through summer and into fall, long after most herbaceous peonies have declined. It tolerates a wider soil pH range and more heat than traditional Paeonia lactiflora cultivars, making it one of the more forgiving peonies for the warmer edge of peony range, though reliable flowering still depends on some winter chilling.

common_name: Cora Louise Itoh Peony (White Lavender-Flared Intersectional Peony)

planting.note: Plant bare-root divisions in fall 4–6 weeks before the ground freezes, with eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Plant roots with the eyes no more than 1–2 in below the soil surface in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving afternoon shade where summers are hottest. Cora Louise bears large, semi-double, near-white flowers brushed with fine violet-purple flares near the center around a boss of gold stamens, a refined, orchid-like combination on a compact, densely branched plant that rarely needs staking. Like other Itoh hybrids it blooms over a longer season than herbaceous peonies because a single stout stem carries multiple buds that open in sequence, and the clean, deeply lobed foliage holds up well through summer heat and humidity. It tolerates more heat and a broader soil pH range than traditional herbaceous peony cultivars, making it a good choice for gardeners at the warmer edge of the peony-growing range who still get enough winter chill to trigger reliable bloom.
